name: Development
description:
What made India embrace the developmental state?  
Chandan Gowda presents his book Longing for an Elsewhere, arguing that this decision was born not from mid-twentieth century decolonization, but rather from colonized elites’ earlier hunger for civilizational recognition through progress. The talk is followed by a panel discussion and audience Q&A. 
Beyond repositioning when development discourse was born, the book argues that culture actively shapes what is often treated as a purely economic process. This is examined through the case of Mysore, the princely state that pursued its own path to development under British indirect rule between 1881 and 1947, tracing the cultural forces that guided its ideas and endeavours. 



Mysore and the Origins of a Modern Obsession

name: A Tale of Two Middle Classes
description:
How has the transformation of the Indian economy over the 21st century shaped the lives of ordinary Indians?  
This talk traces the evolution of India’s middle classes through data from the India Human Development Survey, a study that repeatedly interviewed more than 40,000 households between 2004 and 2024. Grounded in these lived experiences, the talk examines the size and origins of both the upper and lower middle classes, exploring their lifestyles and aspirations as they navigate a changing, and at times uncertain, economy.

name: Crystal & Ash
description:
Are relics more than static remnants of the past? 
This lecture on the relics of the Buddha excavated from the ancient stupa at Piprahwa, traces their long, contested journey to reveal the deep entanglement of material culture, belief, and power across history and into the present. 
Excavated in 1898 and removed from India for over a century, the Piprahwa relics have been shrouded in controversy, from disputes over authenticity to competing claims of ownership and attempted auctions. Their recent return brings new urgency to old questions. Naman P. Ahuja will explain how relics are defined in Buddhist tradition, their role in geopolitics through what scholars call “relic diplomacy,” the legal shifts shaping their custody, and what all this means for museums today.

name: How Far a Note Travels: The Nadhaswaram and a Music Built for Distance
description:
How do you fill a temple town with music, outdoors, with no electricity? 
The answer is a two-and-a-half-foot cone of hardwood with a double reed, played with circular breathing so the sound never stops. Paired with the tavil, a drum of comparable force, the periya melam, the big ensemble, was built to be heard across a moving procession, over crowds, in open air, for hours. 
This listening session spotlights the nadhaswaram, the mangala vadyam, or auspicious instrument, not merely an accompaniment to a sacred occasion but understood as a fundamental part of what makes it sacred. The families who played it, the Isai Vellalar, were classified under the Sudra varna and considered ritually polluting, even as no temple ceremony could proceed without their music. When the microphone arrived in the mid-twentieth century, the acoustic problem the instrument was built to solve disappeared. T.N. Rajarathnam Pillai, the tradition’s greatest player, responded by redesigning it, a longer body, a lower pitch, tone for carrying power. 
The session aims to help listeners hear gamaka, the sliding ornamentation that gives a raga its identity, most audible on the nadhaswaram’s fretless pipe, and traces the instrument’s global cousins, from the Turkish zurna to the Chinese suona, closing with Sheik Chinna Moulana, the Muslim vidwan from a three-century lineage who became Asthana Vidwan at Srirangam and Tirupati. 
Recordings are drawn from the Archive of Indian Music, Smithsonian Folkways and other archival sources, with acknowledgement from the stage. 
BIC’s Listening Room Sessions are an opportunity to come together, listen to and discover new music, refine old tastes and share influences, stories and memories.

name: The Siachen Glacier - Managing Mountains and War
description:
Inside the world’s highest, harshest battlefield, this talk covers not only the mountains but the war, politics, financial cost, and human toll of the ongoing conflict in Siachen. Here, India, Pakistan, and China have been engaged in hostilities for decades. The talk includes over 180 photographs documenting the Siachen Glacier and the people involved. 
Drawing on visits to the region since 1980, including reaching Karakoram Pass, Col Italia, and Indira Col, the three northernmost points of India, the talk traces the Indian Army’s role in the glacier, the young soldiers who serve there, and the sacrifices they make. It considers the challenges civilian expeditions face on the glacier, questions of leadership, and a proposal for a “Siachen Peace Park” to end the conflict. Though a ceasefire holds today, soldiers continue to endure the glacier’s harsh conditions. 
In collaboration with: 
The Himalayan Club
Founded in 1928, the Himalayan Club is one of the earliest mountaineering clubs established in the subcontinent, with a presence across India and abroad. Its objectives extend beyond climbing to publications, awards, lectures, social activities, sponsorships, and mountain film festivals. First published in 1928, The Himalayan Journal has earned worldwide recognition as the most reliable reference on the Himalaya, Karakoram, and Hindukush. Members include some of the most decorated mountaineers and explorers in India and abroad. The club will soon celebrate its centenary year!

name: Beyond ‘I like It’
description:
What makes an artwork meaningful? This talk journeys across cultures, time periods, and artistic mediums to discover how artworks speak in different visual languages, leaving audiences with simple tools to look at the world around with greater curiosity, confidence, and attention. 
The aim of the session is to cultivate visual literacy; the ability to observe carefully, recognize that images are constructed rather than neutral, and appreciate how meaning emerges through the interplay of form, material, history, culture, and the viewer’s own experience. Across cave paintings, temple sculpture, photography, contemporary installations, and even the images encountered every day, the question thus transforms from, “What does this artwork mean?” to, “How is meaning being made here?”

name: Re-Garde
description:
Re-Garde is a contemporary dance piece moving between opposing pairs: youth and old age, control and release. As the choreographers describe it, the piece traces how our way of observing the world, people, art, conflict, each other, transforms from childhood to adulthood, shaped by the societies and environments we inhabit. 
Exploring the sense of sight, the performance follows two performers as mirrors of each other’s projections, ready to give, lose, provoke and be provoked; crossing the delicate boundaries that separate them, suspended between gesture and poetry. What does it mean to look at the world clear-sighted, unconditioned, free?  
MF Company:
MF Company is a contemporary dance and physical theatre company founded by Maxime Freixas and Francesco Colaleo. Since 2014, they’ve performed internationally across festivals in France, Italy, Poland, Spain, Germany and beyond, exploring humorous, physical and committed research of the body, rhythm and dynamic space. They have been supported by DRAC ARA, the French Institute (FR, MA, PL, IT, HU), the Metropolis and the City of Lyon.

name: Decoding Behavioural Insights
description:
Incentives and institutions, culture and power — this panel discussion examines the intersection of behavioural science, public purpose, and corporate decision-making in contemporary India, centred around Sutapa Banerjee’s new book The Business of Business is (Not) Just Business. 
Behavioural economics, the study of judgement and decision-making, has a rich academic history and practical applications across nearly every part of human experience. As public policy think tanks and corporate consultancies increasingly adopt and adapt this research, understanding its core principles has become more important than ever. Drawing on examples from the Indian context, the panel illustrates the relevance and multidisciplinary reach of behavioural insights in shaping both institutions and everyday decisions.

name: Working Girls
description:
133 min | Tamil, Hindi, Bangla, Marathi, Malayalam and Telugu with English subtitles | 2005 
Invisible women, seen through the lens of wit, humour and dignity. 
Domestic workers, farmers, mothers, ASHA workers, dancers, and organisers all labour to sustain society but are rarely acknowledged. Working Girls is a vivid, genre-defying documentary that traverses India to uncover the invisible yet essential work performed by women. From care work and domestic work to surrogacy and sex work, the film challenges dominant ideas about labour, value, and visibility. 
It was filmed across the country in Kolkata, Mumbai, Shillong, Latur, Thiruvananthapuram, Hyderabad and Madurai. The film is directed by Paromita Vohra and created in collaboration with the Laws of Social Reproduction project. The Laws of Social Reproduction project, led by Prabha Kotiswaran at King’s College London, draws on feminist legal theory to study women’s reproductive labour, and how law renders this labour invisible, proposing reform toward economic justice for women.

name: Antarnaad
description:
The call of the soul can be heard this evening. 
Rakshit Kulkarni’s recital features two Hindustani rāgas, presented in their traditional depth and grandeur. This is followed by a selection of rare Haridasa compositions in the second half of the concert. He is accompanied by Mihir Kalyanpur on tabla and Anjana Hegde on harmonium. 
The Haridasa tradition began in Karnataka centuries ago, blossoming from the Dvaita philosophy of Madhvacharya. Saint-composers like Purandara Dasa and Kanaka Dasa wrote devotional songs in Kannada, making sacred philosophy accessible to ordinary people. These compositions were originally sung in the Carnatic style, but over time, particularly in North Karnataka, Hindustani music began to shape how Haridasa songs were rendered. Vocalists like Bhimsen Joshi carried this crossover forward, and it continues today. This recital brings together both traditions, presenting Haridasa compositions through a Hindustani lens.

name: Losing Words, Losing Worlds
description:
If you can predict it, you can name it. 
Across India, hundreds of words in local dialects capture the specific rhythms of regional climate: a short drizzle versus a multi-day downpour, particular cloud formations, the first signs of a temperature spike. This talk looks at what it means when those words start to disappear, and what that loss says about our relationship to the natural world. 
India’s climate discourse is largely conducted in English, top-down, and removed from the lived reality of those most affected by the crisis. As weather patterns grow more erratic, the environmental phenomena they once reliably described are disappearing too, and with them, the language and knowledge. A pilot study across twenty-two languages and fifteen states found that farmers, fisherfolk, and forest-dependent communities report over a hundred vernacular terms fading from use, taking entire systems of ecological literacy with them. Language, this project argues, is infrastructure essential to grassroots resilience and locally grounded climate solutions. 
Venue: Seminar Halls
